title: Back-end development
description: Review the services, APIs, data stores and jobs behind the product: contracts, data integrity, failure handling and server-side security.
expertises: Background jobs, integrations and failure handling
questions: Which services, endpoints, tables and jobs does the change touch, and who calls them?
What happens to data if a request is retried, interrupted or runs twice at the same time?
How is the change deployed and rolled back when the database schema changes?

specialists.title: API contract engineer
specialists.focus: Check changed endpoints, events and webhooks against their contract and their consumers, and decide whether the change is compatible or needs a new version.
checks: The contract file is updated in the same change and validated in CI.
Removing or renaming a field, or making one required, is treated as breaking and versioned or deprecated.
Unsafe methods that clients retry are idempotent or take an idempotency key.

specialists.title: Data integrity engineer
specialists.focus: Identify the invariants, the transaction boundaries and the isolation level each write needs, and what happens on retry, crash or concurrent writes.
checks: Each multi-step write runs in one transaction or has a compensating action.
The isolation level is chosen on purpose; PostgreSQL's default is Read Committed.
Uniqueness and foreign keys are enforced by the database, not only by application code.

specialists.title: Schema migration engineer
specialists.focus: Plan schema and data migrations that run without downtime and that the previous application version tolerates during the rollout.
checks: Migrations follow expand then contract: add, backfill, switch readers, then remove.
Long locks are avoided on large tables; the migration is timed on a production-sized copy.
The rollback path is written, including what happens to data written by the new version.

specialists.title: Server-side security engineer
specialists.focus: Check object-level and property-level authorization on each endpoint, input validation and resource limits, the top risks of the OWASP API Security Top 10.
checks: Every endpoint that takes an object ID checks that the caller may access that object.
Responses return only the fields the caller may see; mass assignment of fields is blocked.
Pagination, request size and rate limits bound the resources one caller can consume.

evidence: API contract diff and the list of known consumers.
Migration scripts with their timing on a production-sized dataset and the rollback plan.
Tests for retries, concurrent writes and authorization on each changed endpoint.
Service metrics and logs for the endpoints and jobs the change touches.
challenge: What happens if the same request arrives twice, or two requests change the same record at once?
Can the old and new application versions run against the migrated schema at the same time?
Which consumer of this endpoint did nobody ask about?
Would a simpler design, such as a synchronous call instead of a queue, meet the need?
decision_criteria: Proceed when contracts are compatible or versioned, writes keep their invariants under retry and concurrency, and migrations are reversible.
Revise when a migration locks a large table, a breaking contract change has no deprecation path or an endpoint lacks object-level authorization.
Ask for a staged rollout or a dual-write period when data moves between stores or schemas.
Name the back-end metric, such as error rate, p95 latency or queue age, and the threshold that triggers rollback.
